Start with the job

A useful shortlist starts with what you need to ship

Deploying a token is only the beginning. A financial product can still fail at the first redemption, lost wallet or upgrade. Choose the team that can demonstrate the difficult workflow, not the one with the longest list of blockchain logos.

Quick answer: compare custom builders such as Minddeft, protocol-oriented groups such as ChainSafe and Wonderland, infrastructure and security engineering from Nethermind, and integration work from Protofire. For a separate security assessment, evaluate OpenZeppelin, Ackee Blockchain and Trail of Bits against the actual codebase. Frameworks, oracle networks and monitoring products support these teams; they are not interchangeable development agencies.

How this shortlist works

FluidRWA groups options by delivery role, public technical material, project scope and the questions a buyer must resolve. The order is not a quality score. The selected engineering profiles and primary references below were reviewed on November 23, 2026. Public documentation establishes described capabilities, not delivery performance on your project. We have not run a hands-on benchmark or collected a comparable client-review dataset for these companies.

Chain and language

Hire for your execution environment, not a generic multichain claim

EVM: Solidity, Vyper and layer 2 environments

Ask for work on your target network and the exact compiler and dependency versions proposed. Compare contract permissions, proxy design, oracle assumptions and external integrations. Moving familiar Solidity code to a different EVM network does not reproduce the original custody integrations, liquidity or operating environment. Ask who owns RPC access, indexing, transaction retries and failed submissions.

For an upgradeable system, request the proxy type, initializer controls, storage-layout checks and a rehearsal using realistic existing state. An immutable implementation needs a different migration and incident plan. Neither model is automatically the right choice for every product.

Solana: programs, data accounts and authority

Solana's documentation separates executable programs from mutable data accounts. A buyer should therefore request account-validation tests and a clear map of signer, owner and upgrade-authority checks, rather than accepting an EVM audit checklist with the chain name changed. Ask about cross-program interactions and how the system handles unexpected accounts or instructions.

Clarify whether the team uses Anchor, native Rust or another supported approach and why. Review the program deployment and verification process. Removing an upgrade authority changes future recovery options, so make that an explicit product decision with a rehearsal, not a checkbox hidden in deployment.

Move, Cairo and specialist environments

Do not treat a language appearing on a sales page as demonstrated delivery experience. Ask the candidate to walk through a relevant repository, the target chain's asset model, test setup and reviewer availability. Aptos and Sui are not interchangeable simply because both use Move. The same applies to specialist execution environments and their deployment procedures.

Keep the proof proportional to the engagement. A small paid discovery milestone can establish a demonstrable architecture and integration prototype before a full delivery commitment. The milestone should produce something your own engineers can inspect and continue using.

Permissioned and enterprise networks

Start with who participates, who sees each record and who can change network policy. Known participants do not eliminate access-control mistakes, compromised keys or integration failures. Ask how membership, identity, data retention, upgrades and operational support work when organizations disagree or a participant exits.

Public networks, private frameworks and contract-management software solve different problems. A document-signing or legal-agreement workflow is not automatically a blockchain smart contract platform. Choose the deployment model from the business requirement, then assess teams that can implement it.

Technical reference: Solana programs documentation. The other items in this section are FluidRWA procurement questions, not vendor performance claims.

Evidence before promises

Trace a proposed capability to something you can inspect

A polished case study is a lead, not the end of diligence. Build a short evidence chain from the claimed work to the people, code and release you are considering. Confidential projects can use a permissioned reference call or a redacted review; confidentiality should not prevent a precise explanation of what the supplier actually delivered.

  1. Identify the contribution

    Record the product, chain, deployment date, relevant repository or release, and the supplier's role. Did the team design the protocol, implement one module, build the front end or perform an audit? Ask a reference to confirm that specific contribution. A logo wall cannot answer this.

  2. Connect the code to the release

    Request the repository commit, dependency lockfile, compiler settings, deployment manifest and contract addresses. Have a technical reviewer reproduce the build and check how the deployed implementation corresponds to that release. A block explorer's verified-source label helps inspect code; it is not an audit or proof of business correctness.

  3. Connect the review to the same scope

    Read the audit's commit, files, dates, assumptions, exclusions and unresolved findings. Compare the release manifest with what was reviewed. If a proxy points to a newer implementation, or configuration changed after review, ask what additional testing or review covered the difference.

  4. Inspect the people who will do the work

    Ask for named technical leads, seniority, time allocation and substitution rules. Separate employees, subcontractors and independent reviewers. Confirm who can answer difficult architecture questions without routing every answer through sales. An organization-level open-source track record does not establish the proposed team's availability.

  5. Test handover before depending on it

    Have your own team run the test suite, deploy to a controlled environment and follow the operational instructions. Confirm access to source, CI configuration, deployment records and documentation. The supplier should not be the only party capable of shipping a fix or explaining a privileged action.

What the evidence does and does not prove

A published repository proves that material is available to inspect. An audit report describes a bounded review. A reference can confirm an engagement. None of these establishes that a new deployment is risk-free. Compare the same artifacts across candidates and document the remaining decision, rather than converting marketing metrics into a security score.

Acceptance, not just a demo

Make every candidate prove the same difficult actions

A happy-path demo hides the expensive decisions. Give shortlisted teams the same small scenario and ask them to explain both the expected result and the evidence they would deliver. The following is a buyer's acceptance template, not a certification or a claim that every listed provider offers every control.

Example acceptance tests to adapt with your technical and business owners
AreaDemonstrationArtifact to retain
PermissionsAn ordinary wallet cannot mint, pause, upgrade or modify eligibility; an authorized role can perform only its documented actions.Role matrix, negative tests and transaction traces.
Financial logicDeposits, withdrawals, fees and rounding follow the specification under partial balances and repeated operations.Accounting examples, invariant tests and reconciliation results.
External dependenciesA failed call, delayed data update or unavailable automation service produces a defined outcome rather than silent success.Dependency inventory, failure tests and fallback policy.
UpgradesA proposed release preserves required state and permissions; unauthorized upgrades fail.Storage review, migration tests, approval record and rehearsal.
MonitoringA simulated privileged change or abnormal event reaches the correct responder, who follows the approved response procedure.Alert event, delivery receipt, runbook and response log.
Exit and recoveryThe buyer can deploy, rotate credentials and operate without the original delivery team.Handover checklist, recovery exercise and access inventory.

Ask the team to explain its threat model before listing tools. Static analysis, unit tests, fuzzing and independent manual review answer different questions. Formal verification can examine specified properties, but the chosen specification and assumptions still matter. A high coverage number does not by itself demonstrate that critical economic or permission failures were tested.

Use OWASP's Smart Contract Top 10 to structure a discussion of access control, oracle manipulation, business logic, input validation, reentrancy and other documented risks. Add project-specific tests instead of treating a generic checklist as a complete review. Discuss private data and public execution carefully: a Solidity variable marked private is not a promise of confidential onchain information.

Primary reference for the last point: Solidity security considerations. For an independent assessment shortlist, see security audit companies.

A tokenized-asset example

Follow the investor journey all the way through redemption

Imagine a fund issuer that has selected an asset and wants a branded investor portal. The token contract is only the visible tip of the project. Before hiring, walk a candidate through these connected stages and ask where its implementation scope ends.

1. Eligibility becomes an enforceable state

A business operator determines eligibility under its chosen framework. The application then needs an authorized way to associate an approved investor with an allowed wallet and to change that status later. Ask how expiry, revocation, a lost wallet and a wrongly approved record propagate to transfer permissions. Avoid putting unnecessary personal documents directly onchain.

2. Money and tokens reconcile

Define when an order is accepted, when funds are considered received and who authorizes issuance. Test duplicate messages, partial settlement, wrong references and cancellations. The customer ledger, onchain supply and servicing records should have a documented reconciliation process. A webhook firing once in a demo is not a production settlement design.

3. Holding and transfer rules survive change

Ask what happens when a holder's status changes, a destination wallet is ineligible, or an authorized operator must freeze or recover a position. ERC-3643 describes identity and compliance interfaces for restricted token transfers, among other controls. Choosing a standard is a technical starting point, not a substitute for designing and reviewing your particular rules.

4. Distributions and redemptions close the loop

Specify record dates, calculation inputs, failed payouts, reconciliation and corrections. A redemption may require offchain approval and asset liquidity before tokens can be burned or proceeds delivered. State what the investor sees during a delay and who resolves an exception. Do not promise instant redemption merely because a contract function executes quickly.

Keep an ownership table for the issuer, development team, investor-onboarding provider, custodian, administrator and security reviewer. Assign who approves rules, who implements them, who holds keys, who monitors failures and who communicates with investors. The developer should implement agreed requirements, not silently decide legal rights or investor eligibility.

Primary standard: ERC-3643 specification. Compare adjacent KYC and AML providers and custody providers when the implementation crosses those boundaries.

Different products, different proofs

Adapt the evaluation to what the contract actually does

Two teams may both advertise DeFi development while solving very different engineering problems. Use these examples to turn an industry label into a concrete evaluation. They are hypothetical buyer scenarios, not claims of completed client projects by the companies in the directory.

Lending, staking and vault products

Ask the candidate to specify collateral accounting, withdrawals, rewards, fees and external data assumptions before showing the interface. Choose a failure example: a delayed price update, a large withdrawal or a downstream protocol that stops accepting deposits. Request a trace of what the user owns and can redeem at each stage. The useful evidence is the accounting specification and tests, not a generic DeFi portfolio category.

NFTs, gaming and marketplaces

Define ownership and permissions separately from the visual experience. Ask what stays onchain, where media or metadata lives, which operator can change it and what happens if an application server disappears. For a marketplace, distinguish listing, authorization, transfer and payment failure paths. For a game, identify which actions need onchain settlement and which are ordinary application events. Do not mistake token creation for a complete commercial or player experience.

Supply-chain, escrow and enterprise workflows

Start with the event that releases an obligation and the person or system allowed to attest to it. A contract cannot independently establish that an offchain delivery happened. Ask how disputes, incorrect input, duplicate messages and a missing participant are handled. The evaluation should connect the external evidence, authorized decision and onchain result, with a retained audit trail.

Cross-chain systems and migrations

Write down the source of truth and the dependency that carries a message or asset between environments. Ask the team to demonstrate delayed, repeated and failed processing without creating duplicate balances. For a migration, define how existing holders, approvals, positions and historical records are reconciled. Request a cutover rehearsal and a documented fallback decision before the production date.

A short technical interview that exposes the real scope

Pick one scenario and ask the proposed lead to draw the system, name the trust boundaries and identify the first three things that could go wrong. Then ask which tests would detect those failures and who would act on the alert. Follow with a change request: a new custody provider, a revoked investor or an unavailable signer. A strong discussion makes dependencies and limits easier to inspect; it does not rely on promising that nothing can fail.

Retain that discussion as agreed requirements. If candidates make different assumptions, resolve them before comparing delivery proposals. This often creates a more useful shortlist than adding another ten companies with the same generic description.

Your project brief

Get proposals you can actually compare

Send every candidate the same brief. That prevents one proposal covering a bare contract while another includes the portal, integrations and operating support. Use these headings as a working outline, then ask suppliers to answer each one rather than submitting an unrelated capabilities deck.

  1. Product, users and boundaries

    Describe the user journey, asset or protocol, target chain, currencies, expected transaction patterns and jurisdictions involved. State what already exists and what is out of scope. Identify whether the supplier is responsible for contracts only, a full application, infrastructure, a migration or ongoing operations.

  2. Roles and difficult business rules

    List ordinary users and privileged actors. Explain minting, transfers, withdrawals, fees, pause, upgrades and recovery. Include the actions that must fail. If a business rule is undecided, make discovery a separate deliverable with an accountable decision-maker rather than asking the engineer to guess.

  3. Integrations and data

    Name the wallet, custody, oracle, identity, payment and reporting systems you expect to use. Ask suppliers to identify compatibility assumptions and partner dependencies. Specify how data is reconciled and who investigates a mismatch. Request a data-flow diagram covering sensitive information as well as onchain events.

  4. Testing, review and release gates

    State the required test artifacts, deployment rehearsal and independent security review. Ask for an audit-ready code freeze, time for fixes and a retest gate. Make production approval depend on accepted evidence, not merely the end of a calendar milestone.

  5. Ownership, documentation and support

    Cover source ownership, licensing, subcontractors, access, key custody and handover. Specify support coverage, response expectations and escalation contacts. Define the difference between a defect, a new feature, a dependency change and an incident. Require a usable exit plan and access removal at the end of the engagement.

Which engagement model makes sense?

A scoped project works when requirements and acceptance criteria are stable. A dedicated team can suit a changing roadmap if you have product ownership and technical oversight. Team extension fills a defined skill gap under your engineering management. Discovery followed by delivery is useful when architecture or integration risk is still uncertain. In each case, distinguish development, independent review and ongoing operation in the proposal.

What drives effort and timing?

Novel financial logic, cross-chain interactions, upgradeability, legacy-state migration, external integrations and evidence requirements usually create more work than deploying a standard token. Include documentation, independent review, remediation, deployment and support in the scope comparison. Ask for milestone assumptions and resource dependencies; do not compare an all-in production engagement with a prototype estimate.

Agency, specialist or independent developer?

A capable independent engineer can be appropriate for a bounded task with strong buyer oversight. A multidisciplinary firm may help when contracts, backend, interface and operations must move together. Neither structure guarantees better work. Test key-person dependence, review independence, documentation and cover during absence. Ask who can maintain the system if the original author leaves.

Does location matter?

Use location to check working-hour overlap, contracting entity, communication, data handling and access requirements. Do not use a country or region as a proxy for security quality. A distributed team can work well with clear ownership and review practices; an office near you does not replace a tested release process.

From shortlist to release

Use milestones that leave the buyer in control

The most useful project plan is not a line saying development followed by launch. It tells both sides which decisions must be made, what evidence will be produced and who can stop the release. Adapt this example to your product; it is a procurement framework, not a universal development timeline.

Discovery: resolve the unknowns that change the build

Ask for a system diagram, user and operator journeys, dependency list and a decision log. The output should explain whether custom contracts are needed at all. Identify unresolved asset rights, integration access or business rules that prevent implementation. A discovery phase is complete when you can approve a bounded implementation scope or make an informed decision not to proceed.

Keep the deliverables usable outside the original agency. Require the diagram and specification in accessible formats, identify the authors and record assumptions. This avoids paying for another discovery exercise simply because a different team takes over.

Implementation: make progress inspectable

Use a buyer-accessible repository and a working review process from the start. Ask for small demonstrable increments tied to the specification, not screenshots of progress. A useful milestone might show a restricted transfer working and an unauthorized transfer failing, with tests that your own reviewer can run.

Track assumptions that change during implementation. If the custody interface or oracle choice changes, update the system diagram, tests and responsibilities. A growing collection of exceptions outside the specification is a warning that the acceptance criteria no longer describe the product being built.

Independent review: freeze a scope, not an aspiration

Agree which release and components are ready for the independent reviewer. Deliver the specification, dependency inventory, tests and known issues along with code. Ask the reviewer to identify exclusions and assumptions rather than leaving the buyer to infer them from a report title.

Reserve a remediation stage. Each finding needs an owner, a resolution or a documented acceptance decision, and an appropriate retest. Record changes made after review and decide whether they reopen the review scope. A report delivered before substantial code changes cannot stand in for a review of the final release.

Release and handover: prove operational readiness

Run the deployment procedure in a controlled environment and retain its manifest. Confirm the intended configuration and authorities, monitor the important events and rehearse escalation. Have the buyer's operator perform the steps with the instructions supplied, rather than watching the vendor's engineer do everything.

Complete an access review after handover. Remove unnecessary vendor permissions, identify retained support access and test credential rotation. The buyer should know how to authorize the next release and recover from an unavailable supplier before production depends on either action.

A concrete proposal comparison

Suppose Proposal A offers a token contract and Proposal B offers a contract, portal and custody integration. The difference is not resolved by comparing their company size. Put the deliverables into the same columns: contract functions, interface, integrations, test artifacts, security review, deployment, documentation and support. Mark included, excluded or dependent on another agreement. Ask both teams to answer the missing items.

Next, give both teams the same exception: an approved investor changes wallets while a subscription is pending. Ask how the identity record, allowed wallet, payment reference, token issuance and customer communication stay consistent. The objective is not a free finished design. It is to expose which parts of the workflow each team understands, which assumptions it needs and who must decide the remaining questions.

Keep a handover inventory

Retain source and licenses, dependency versions, build instructions, tests, deployment addresses, admin roles, signer policy, external-service accounts, monitoring rules, incident contacts and a change log. Add data exports and reconciliation instructions for offchain records. Assign an owner to each item and ask the receiving team to confirm that it can actually use it.

Separate credentials from the general project documents and agree a secure transfer procedure. Do not put secrets into a public repository or an emailed handover deck. The inventory should state who controls an account and how access is recovered without exposing the credential itself.

Decide what would make you walk away

Before the final call, agree which conditions are non-negotiable: access to your source, documented admin control, an appropriate independent review, a credible target-chain reference or the ability to operate after handover. A team may be a competent supplier and still not meet your specific requirements. Document that distinction instead of turning every selection into an unsupported best-company ranking.

Make the decision

A practical scorecard for your shortlist

Have product, engineering and operations review the same shortlist. Mark each item demonstrated, partially demonstrated or not yet demonstrated, attach an artifact and record the remaining action. This is a template for your decision, not FluidRWA's numerical rating of the companies.

  • Comparable scope: a reference confirms the proposed team's contribution to relevant work, including what it did not deliver.
  • Technical fit: the team explains the target environment, dependencies and a credible reason for the architecture.
  • Security process: the threat model, testing, independent review and remediation responsibilities are explicit.
  • Operational control: production keys, alerts, pause powers, upgrades and recovery belong to named owners.
  • Delivery clarity: milestones have inspectable acceptance criteria, assumptions and change-control rules.
  • Continuity: your team can access, build, deploy and maintain the system after handover.

Red flags worth stopping for

Pause if a candidate cannot distinguish its own work from a client's entire platform, offers an audit guarantee without scope, refuses meaningful access to your source, leaves production administration undocumented, or treats a library audit as coverage of every customization. Be cautious with unconditional claims such as hack-proof, automatically compliant or guaranteed liquidity.

Ask for a concrete example rather than arguing about a slogan. A useful answer might be a redacted audit, a demonstration of a failed unauthorized action or an introduction to a reference. If evidence cannot be shared, decide whether a smaller discovery engagement can resolve the risk before committing to production delivery.

Keep security separate from commercial reputation

Client reviews help assess communication and delivery experience. Repository activity helps inspect engineering practice. Neither alone establishes the security of a new financial system. Likewise, a large company, a popular framework or a familiar brand may still be the wrong fit for a specialist chain or a narrow integration. Use the evidence that matches the actual decision.

After the launch

Own the next upgrade, outage and handover before the first release

Ask what happens on an ordinary Tuesday after the launch team has moved on. Someone must notice a failing dependency, investigate an abnormal transaction and decide whether a response is authorized. A monitoring dashboard without an accountable operator is not an operating model.

Run a response rehearsal

Simulate an unexpected privileged change or unavailable external service in a safe environment. Check alert routing, escalation, decision authority and recovery instructions. Where pause functionality exists, define its limits and who can resume. A pause is not a universal reversal mechanism and may affect users differently across integrated systems.

Make upgrades reviewable

Maintain a release record with code, configuration, dependency changes, tests, approvals and addresses. Identify when a change needs an additional independent review. Treat emergency changes as a governed process with retained evidence, not permission for a supplier to make undocumented production edits.

A current tooling check: hosted Defender has retired

Older hiring guides still recommend setting up OpenZeppelin Defender as a hosted operating layer. OpenZeppelin's official sunset FAQ says the hosted service was retired on July 1, 2026. Its current documentation includes open-source Relayer and Monitor. A new proposal needs to explain the actual deployment and operator, not reuse an obsolete product assumption.

For any self-hosted component, assign hosting, credentials, RPC connections, upgrades, logs, alert channels and availability. Check feature fit rather than assuming a like-for-like migration. Also check the maintenance status of proposed client libraries: ChainSafe announced Web3.js archival for March 4, 2025. A historical contribution can demonstrate past engineering work without being a currently maintained dependency choice.

Primary sources: OpenZeppelin Defender sunset FAQ, current OpenZeppelin tools documentation, ChainSafe Web3.js sunset announcement.

Buyer questions

Smart contract development: questions before you commit

Which smart contract development company is best?

The best fit depends on the job. Compare Minddeft for custom application delivery, ChainSafe and Wonderland for protocol-oriented work, Nethermind for infrastructure and security-heavy engineering, and Protofire for onchain integration. These are starting points, not a universal ranking. Confirm chain-specific work, named engineers and the same acceptance tests with every candidate.

What is the difference between a developer and an auditor?

A developer implements the system. An auditor reviews a defined scope and records findings. An internal review by the builder is useful but is not an independent assessment. State the reviewer, code commit, exclusions, remediation and retest work explicitly.

What determines the effort required for smart contract development?

The main drivers are novel business logic, number of integrations, chain and language, upgradeability, migration requirements, testing, independent review and operating support. Ask candidates to estimate the same written scope and list assumptions, exclusions and change-control rules. A token deployment and a production financial workflow are different engagements.

How long does a smart contract project take?

There is no reliable universal timeline. Separate discovery, implementation, integration, testing, independent review, remediation, deployment rehearsal and handover. Ask for dependencies and acceptance criteria for each milestone. An auditor's availability or an unfinished custody integration can become the critical path even after the code is written.

Does audited code mean a project is safe?

No. An audit covers a particular version and scope under stated assumptions. Changes after review, configuration, admin keys, economic design, external data and offchain services can introduce additional risk. Match the deployed release to the reviewed code and maintain monitoring and response ownership after launch.

Can I use a template or no-code tool instead of hiring developers?

A maintained template can help with standard functionality. Custom permissions, migration, financial accounting and integration behavior still need design and testing. Check the exact template version, modifications, deployment configuration and who can administer it. A no-code interface does not remove responsibility for the deployed contract.

Should I use Ethereum, an EVM layer 2, Solana or a permissioned network?

Choose from user access, asset requirements, privacy, custody support, settlement assumptions and operating constraints. EVM portability does not make bridges, sequencers or oracle dependencies identical. Solana has a different account and program model. A permissioned network still needs governance and integration work. Require evidence on your actual target environment.

Who should control the admin and upgrade keys?

The project should explicitly assign authority and recovery procedures. Document owners, signers, thresholds, timelocks, pause powers and key rotation. A vendor should not retain undeclared production control. Test the handover and emergency process, including what happens if one signer is unavailable.

Does a token standard make a real-world asset offering compliant?

No. A standard can express technical controls such as transfer checks, identity registries or restricted actions. It does not establish the asset's legal rights, investor eligibility, offering permissions or the responsibilities of regulated intermediaries. Those decisions need qualified advisers and accountable business operators.

Is OpenZeppelin Defender still available for a new deployment?

Hosted OpenZeppelin Defender was retired on July 1, 2026. OpenZeppelin's current documentation includes open-source Relayer and Monitor. Evaluate migration and operating responsibilities rather than assuming an old proposal's hosted Defender workflow is still available.
